utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. Yes, Counsel Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Maybe this is not the right moment, but that is up to you to judge, but Defence counsel would have an observation to make in connection with the list of witnesses supplied by the Prosecutor, claiming that he doesn't have enough information about them. So some of the Defence counsel would like to comment briefly on that list if it may please Your Honour, if this is the moment or at some other point in time. It will only take a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We consider that it is more appropriate to deal with this matter after we have completed the examination-in-chief of this witness. So if you don't mind, we would put off this discussion until we are through with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: We accept your suggestion, Your Honour. ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed) Examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Cilic. We will resume where we broke off yesterday. So after you were in Busovaca at the press conference, you returned where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned to the command of the Viteska Brigade in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the situation like there as you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned, my obligation being to inform immediately the command of the Viteska Brigade about what we had learned at the press conference, and to edit that information for the local media, the radio station and the TV station. Also, to prepare reports for members of the local commands and for the media that a number of us were working for, that is the Croatian media in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, two extremely alarming reports reached us. This was in the afternoon. One was that in the area of the Kuber feature, it is a part of Busovaca municipality bordering on Vitez and Zenica, a serious armed incident had occurred between members of the BH army and HVO troops. Namely, at that elevation point members of the Croatian Defence Council had captured that point after the attack on Busovaca after the 25th of January, 1993. This was a disturbing incident, because that day there were so many such bad reports that this was just another one that added fuel to the flames. In the afternoon a report reached us that all road communication between Vitez and Zenica had been broken off, that members of the Zenica MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which at that time was exclusively composed of Muslims, and members of the BH army had blocked the road and there was no way of going into or leaving Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do then in view of this situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This disturbed me in particular, because my 17-year-old daughter was attending third grade of secondary school, a language school, in Zenica. For the first two years she travelled to Zenica by bus every morning and came back in the same way in the evening. However, when she started third year studies, that is the autumn of '92, because of the different political and security situation and also due to the shortage of oil and oil derivatives, traffic was irregular between Vitez and Zenica as well as the other areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the reason why we had to find accommodation for our daughter, and that is what we did. We found a room for her with a family in Zenica, and she would come home only during the weekend. Sometimes she would skip a weekend because simply there was no transport. Of course, as a father this alarmed me because there are already been incidents in Busovaca, then this one at Kuber, the murder of the escort of Commander Totic, and so I decided to try to reach Zenica and bring my daughter home. Let me add, in passing, that I had a very difficult problem the year previously when my older daughter happened to be in Sarajevo, and again it was a real adventure to reach Sarajevo and back. So I hoped that good luck and the All Mighty would help me bring my daughter back home. So I don't know whether I need to explain this in detail. I did manage to bring my daughter home. If necessary, I can convey some of the interesting things that happened to me and that I saw on the road from Vitez to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, the road to Zenica was blocked; wasn't it? Would you tell us who put up the roadblocks and who was manning them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received permission from the commander of the Viteska Brigade, Mario Cerkez, to go and fetch my daughter to Busovaca -- sorry, to Zenica, though he did so hesitantly because of the incidents that had occurred. However, I insisted, and he didn't find it in his heart to prevent me from getting my child from Zenica. To reach Zenica you have to cross a pass, about 12 or 13 kilometres long at Veternica, the pass is called Veternica, and there were no vehicles except for one or two coming from the direction of Zenica, which gave me faith that the road would be open. Later on, however, it emerged that this was not so, but that certain vehicles that couldn't reach Zenica or pass through Zenica would make an U-turn and return to Vitez. This part of the road through Vitez municipality I managed to cross unhindered after passing through barricades. One was at the turnoff towards Zenica, which was manned by the civilian police, by a Croatian policeman from Vitez. The second roadblock was at the top of the Veternica pass, on the boarder between Vitez and Zenica municipalities. There were two policemen there, civilian policemen. I knew one of them well because he was a member of the Vitez police station, and he let me pass without any problems and continue my journey to Zenica, warning me that I wouldn't be able to reach it because there was a long line of cars already that had formed towards Zenica and that were at a standstill and waiting to pass. Thanking him for letting me pass, I continued my journey. I drove around the column because the vehicles were lined up on the right-hand side of the road and there were none on the left-hand side, so I reached the settlement of Cajdras. It is a settlement very close to Zenica, mostly inhabited by Croats, but there is a crossroads where roads lead off to Vitez and Zenica, and to the left a side-road heading towards Travnik via Guca Gora. I think there were about 30 policemen there and members of the HOS, H-O-S. At the time HOS was still functioning in the area of Zenica. It was of mixed ethnic composition with members, Croats and Muslims. I was wearing civilian clothes and I had with me, in addition to my ID card an ID card of the Croatian Defence Council. So I thought to myself how I could make my way to Zenica, and it was a question of 500 or 600 metres. So I decided to show one of the HOS members my ID card of the HVO. I did so. And I must say that I had with me seven or eight boxes of cigarettes with ten packets each. I was carrying them to give them to the family with whom my daughter was staying. There were no cigarettes in Zenica, or if there were any they were much more expensive than in Vitez. Giving him this box and making a very quiet plea, I never really gathered whether he was a Croat or a Muslim, but he was ready to let me pass, saying that at the crossroads itself, known as Sarina, I would not be able to pass because apparently 20 to 30 members of the Zenica MUP were there armed to the teeth. Then another member of the HOS joined in the conversation, and he advised me how I could get into Zenica if I took a turning 200 metres before this point where the MUP members were. There's a stream and a small wooden bridge that small cars can use. Sometimes, you see, it's a good thing to have a small car such as I had at the time. They let me pass, and crossing this bridge I reached Zenica from another direction in relation to the one that was under strict control. At the entry to Zenica, of course this will not mean much to the Court, it is near the church of St. Joseph. I saw there a large group of MUP members armed to the teeth. They were wearing helmets on their heads. They had pistols at their belts and automatic rifles in their hands. They stopped me immediately. I stopped and they asked for papers. I gave them my papers. They examined everything. Of course, I gave them my civilian papers. Then one of them who was checking my documents, cursing the other ones who had let me pass, and, in fact, they hadn't let me pass because I had bypassed them, he asked me where I was going. I explained to them, in pleading terms, I admit that I sought to be as emotional as I could, and I was upset because of my child, and it was only 200 metres from that spot to the place where my daughter was staying. I made a present of a box of cigarettes to him too. They let me pass. I took my daughter, and then we returned along the same route and with only some minor problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see MUP members and members of the BH army in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenica is a very lively transit town, but the situation was most disturbing, the situation I witnessed in Zenica. One couldn't see a civilian. There was no one in the street except for the vehicles of the BH army, the MUP, with their horns on, the sirens on. I saw several vehicles of the MUP as I crossed this path from the entry to the town to the apartment. In agreement with the commander of the Viteska Brigade, Mario Cerkez, my obligation was, when I leave Zenica and head back to Vitez, to let him know that I was on my way back, and this was in the case of any complications or if I should fail to reach Vitez then the commander, through various channels and institutions, would try to trace me if anything happened to me. However, nothing did. This is a trip that doesn't take longer than 20 minutes there and 20 minutes back. It took me about four hours. I reached the headquarters and reported in detail what I had seen. I reported this to Mario Cerkez and some other members of the command who happened to be present in the commander's office at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the time that you did this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could have been about 19.00 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me now show you a document, and you will tell me whether you recognise it or not.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D35/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which corps was based in Zenica and what the strength of the corps was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps was based in Zenica and the commander was Enver Hadzihasanovic. According to estimates that were available to the Vitez Brigade and the Vitez area of responsibility, the 3rd Corps, in the spring of 1993, which means before the escalation of the conflict, numbered up to 30,000 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the area of Vitez belong to the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many brigades the 3rd Corps had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I know that the 325th and the 303rd Brigade was stationed in Vitez at the beginning, but what the total number was I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean at the beginning of the war or during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war and during the war, the 303rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document of the command of the Vitez Brigade obtained from the military intelligence service, dated 10th of April, 1993. Do these data mean anything to you? Actually, the data on the formation of the 325th Mountain Brigade and how it was composed. Apparently there were four battalions and how those battalions were deployed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of us in the command of the Vitez Brigade were more or less familiar with this, precisely from information we received from Tomislav Krizanac, who unfortunately is deceased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it says here that the 4th Battalion, with its command post in Poculica, formed smaller units along the territorial principle. One company for the villages of Poculica, Prnjavor, Vrhovine, and one from Gornja Dubravica, Tolovici, and the village of Sivrino Selo, and one from Pirici, Santici, and Nadoici. The total number of soldiers is 500. Did you have that report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I made -- I cannot be a hundred per cent sure that those figures were exactly the same as these, but we knew that the strongest forces were deployed in the north of Vitez municipality, that is between Vitez and Zenica and those are precisely these places that you have read out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is also stated that the 325th Mountain Brigade was strengthened by Muslim displaced persons. Is that the information you had, that displaced persons joined the Territorial Defence brigades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We all knew this, and being people who whole-heartedly received those displaced persons from Western Bosnia, we were hurt by this. If they didn't stay on in Central Bosnia, their families would go on to Croatia where they were granted refugee status, whereas the able-bodied men stayed behind and joined units of the BH army. And in corroboration of what I'm saying, at the beginning of the war, in the area of the Lasva River Valley, there was a brigade called the Krajina Brigade which was very cruel. This means that they came from Western Bosnia, a part known as Krajina. In fact, the commanders, Mohamed Alagic, who later became corps commander, and his assistant Cuskic, I don't remember his first name, they were former JNA officers and both of them are from Western Bosnia Alagic from Sanski Most, and I don't know about Cuskic, exactly where he came from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the composition of the 325th Mountain Brigade, it follows that the command posts and the individual battalions were all formed on the territorial principle and that they included the inhabitants of various villages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In point 2, it is also stated that the battalion based in Stari Vitez was manned by personnel from Stari Vitez and the town of Vitez. Does this mean that the people were in their villages or in the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A number of them were in Vitez, I don't know whether all of them, but in Old Vitez or Stari Vitez, there were other unit members who were not from the location indicated here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the introductory part, it is also stated that there was a shortage of uniforms on the Muslim side, and that as a result, purchase of hunting clothes, vests and jackets, has been stepped up. Is this something that you yourself noticed, that there was a shortage of uniforms and that there were people wearing civilian clothes on the front?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could very frequently come across people under arms in the streets without military equipment or they might have only a part of it. They might have a jacket but no trousers or boots or vice versa. He may have trousers and no jackets. I think this was a daily phenomenon, there is no question about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you returned to the command of the Vitez Brigade, you informed Commander Mario Cerkez, informed him of what you had seen. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The day before, that is, on the 14th, I was in the command all day performing my regular duties and obligations. In the evening, due to circumstance, that is, the night between the 14th and the 15th, I was on duty together with another colleague member of the command. I was on duty in the Vitez Brigade. This duty implied to stay on after your completed daily shift, which lasted until 20.00 hours, and to remain on duty until 7.00 hours the next day and then continue working that day all day, and then the person who was on duty the previous night would have a night off. That is how it was in my case because I had been on duty for 36 hours non-stop, and after all the problems I had had the previous day, after reporting to the commander, which is normal, I went home to rest and to sleep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now show you a document issued on the 15th of April, 1993, at 10.00 hours by the commander of the Operative Zone, and please tell me whether you saw this document at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D36/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a preparatory combat command for the defence of the HVO in the town of Vitez from extremist Mujahedeen Muslim forces. This order was issued on the 15th of April, 1993, at 10.00 hours. Tell me, did you have access to this document when you returned from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see it in this original form, but I was informed that such a command had arrived from Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was this information conveyed to you? What was the task of the HVO or, rather, the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The task was to increase alertness, to increase the number of men on guard duty, especially command posts, crossroads and so on, and no particular, no special movement of troops was envisaged because the men had -- their military obligation was linked to their place of residence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it necessary to be in combat readiness, to intervene in particular cases, in special circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't have any such orders because I don't believe I would have been sent home to rest if there had been such a command by the commander of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the role of the 4th Military Police Battalion was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 4th Battalion always had specific tasks, and in this order issued by Mr. Tihomir Blaskic, its prime task was to control traffic along the Lasva Valley and to secure the command of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone because it was only some 300 metres away from the confrontation line with the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know then that such a command had been issued to the 4th Military Police Battalion because it was a strategically important road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did know that such an order had been issued because it was the first order of its kind addressed to the command of the 4th Military Police Battalion. Such orders had existed in October 1992 during the first conflict between Croatian and Muslim forces in Ahmici, and whenever tension was running high, the 4th Battalion had more or less the same tasks, that is, to secure the road which was vital to the inhabitants of the Lasva Valley, and to keep it open and free.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The order also mentions, and this is a part of the orders given to the 4th Battalion, that the Ahmici, Pirici, Nadioci, and Ahmici -- if this comes from this direction, if the attack comes from this direction, that they should open fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the locations was at the Bungalow, the Bungalow was one of the points, and I believe that this was put in the order because in this location, this is where the Muslim forces were, and it would have been very easy to shoot even from small arms to the members of -- the Viteska Brigade members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who were the members of the Viteska Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning, this was an HOS formation, which was the first unit which was established in the Lasva Valley, and later on they became a unit, a special purposes unit, as we called them. They were stationed in Vitez and their commander was also from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were also supposed to prevent attacks from the area of Stari Vitez. Did you have any more details on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not have more details, but we did make assessments, if a serious attack had occurred, where, from which direction it would come, so we thought that in Mahala, where a number of well-trained and well-armed soldiers were stationed who were not originally from the area of Mahala and Stari Vitez, we thought that that's where the attack would come from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here you -- it is also specified that -- here it says that -- to be in a state of preparedness to carry out a decisive defence of the territory of the Croatian people. So this was a defensive order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that you can interpret it in different ways. However, what were we to do? We were living in a small valley, we were about 50.000, but we were surrounded by more superior forces, so we could only defend ourselves. So this is how this order was written because we did not have enough forces, not enough men and not enough equipment, to carry out any attacks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please turn to the next page and look at the signature? Is this Tihomir Blaskic's signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the seal that was used by Blaskic, that is, by the commander of the operational zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this time, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just jump to another part, to another issue. We had a document just before this one which was not signed, and this was from the intelligence service of the Viteska Brigade. Why was that document not signed? Was there an obligation to sign documents, these documents that were sent "Strictly Confidential"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were strictly confidential documents but only for internal use, which is why they were not signed, because this document compiled by Mr. Tomislav went directly to Commander Maric, and if he felt it necessary, depending upon the kind of documents, then Mario Cerkez would draft a separate document and send it to particular addressees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did not read out the entire document, but you do know the facts that this document talks about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in all details but generally, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about deployment of troops in the battalions and 325th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. All these locations that are mentioned here mention all the major Muslim villages in the area except for Poculica, which had mixed population, but strategically later it turned out to be very significant because at the Vjetrenice pass, because it is on the Vjetrenice pass between Vitez and Zenica, which is why, from the outset, the conflicts there were very fierce, and the Muslim forces took control of this village, and the other villages are all around Vitez and they are all in a dominant -- they're all dominant features; in other words, they all dominate the area around the city of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to look at another document of 15 April; this is now a bit later, 15.45 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D37/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that I am, even though I could not say so categorically. However, all the facts mentioned here I am familiar with. It just refreshed my memory. Whoever was in the Lasva Valley at that time and who was involved in any information had to have known about 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I don't ask you about the 7th Muslim Brigade, I ask you about the specific document, and the reason why I'm showing you this document is that it is an order issued on 15 April at 15.45, and in paragraph 2, the task of our forces, 2.1, within the zone of responsibility of brigades and for battalions of military police, combat readiness is to be increased to the highest level. Did you have this information? Did you know of that on 15 April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know of this order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you did not know of this order, of which order did you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew of the one which we had talked about before, which was to increase the combat readiness, of the vigilance, and to increase a number of key positions for which the commander thought that they were necessary in their zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you have just said, is that in contradiction with what is stated here? In other words, are you saying the same thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not -- yes, it is not contrary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is what I ask you. Something that is linked to that original order is also mentioned here. Was that the same order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's the same. I think that everything that was in this order -- everything that we did issued out of this order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said that you did not know this order, but everything that you mentioned, it speaks about the same thing, the combat readiness, and I don't ask you anything else. Can you tell me, do you recognise the signature of Colonel Tihomir Blaskic and do you recognise the seal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The order also mentions certain tasks of the information, political work, and its task is defined, is that all members in all units are to be informed on a regular basis about developments within the zone of responsibility and in a broader area. In order to secure quicker and more information flow and exchange of information, full co-operation is to be established with the officer of IPD and the headquarters of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia. Is that task any different from the task that you usually had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I even said that after I returned from Busovaca where the assistant commander for political work, Marko Prskalo, who is an assistant to Commander Blaskic, we had worked on the tasks which the members of the command structure which were in charge of political work, which involved detailed information from the press conferences and information on all the events which took place in the zone of responsibility of our brigade and the Central Bosnia operational zone, I did this immediately after I returned from Zenica, that same afternoon, and I forwarded it to the members in the local command structures, so that this task was fully implemented, and it covered the information that we had received in Busovaca at the press conference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that your regular duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was one of my main tasks, to inform soldiers in a timely fashion on all events in the area in which our brigade was operating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I would like you to look at another document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D38/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you reviewed the documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, you said that on the 16th, that is, the evening of the 15th, the night between the 15th and 16th, you were not in the brigade. Did you see this document during the day of the 17th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is on the 16th during the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps not the original order, but I knew about the contents of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In item 2, "The task of your forces to occupy the defence region to block the villages and prevent all entrances and exits from the villages. In the event of an open attack by the Muslims, neutralise them and prevent their movement by accurate fire from small arms weapons." Also, the deployment of forces is mentioned, which is connected to the previous reports. In other words, did you have this information insisting that these things were going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These events were unfolding when I arrived in the command headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you have any feedback from the field that this was the development when you arrived at work on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps not immediately, but later on it turned out that this was true because in several locations these military operations had been initiated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you learn about this order to block the villages and to return fire in the case of attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that the fire was to be returned if there was an attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Point 4, it says, "Personally responsible to me for the execution of the given task is the commander of the HVO brigade in Vitez Mr. Mario Cerkez." Do you know when he received this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, the order has a heading, this order of 01.30 hours on the 16th, which is a combat command order to prevent attack activity by the enemy extremist Muslim forces and blockade of the broader territory of Kruscica, Vranjske and Donja Verceska, in your view was this an order to attack or an order for an active defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This could only be an order for active defence, because in the villages which are mentioned here, we knew and we saw from the previous documents, well-equipped and armed Muslim forces were deployed. So there was a threat of an incursion deep into the territory and even into the town of Vitez itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the seal of the Central Bosnia operational zone? In other words, do you know what seal this is and do you recognise Blaskic's signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise Blaskic's signature, but the seal is -- cannot be really seen and I don't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we do not have better copies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But based on some details, I could infer that this was the seal used at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Travnik is also mentioned. Why was Travnik still part of that seal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The defence office in Travnik was still operational in some way. The major changes had not yet occurred, and perhaps there were no reasons to change. Only later did the seals change and names of the organisations and institutions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. When did you arrive at the brigade, that is at the command post in the Croatian centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I live about 250 metres away from the command centre, which at that time was the command post of the Vitez Brigade. Sometime right after 5.30, maybe twenty to six I could hear the first loud detonation, and before that we had a verbal and written order that in case of any emergency we were to immediately report to the command post. As the situation was very tense the day before, these first explosions were enough of a signal for me to rush to the command post, and I was there, I believe, before 6.00 a.m. While crossing that short distance I heard explosions from various locations. I could hear them within this town's limits, and it was clear to me that these were not regular acts of provocation but that something more serious was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I arrived at the command post, I believe, between ten to six and five to six. It was before 6.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whom did you find there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most members of the command were there, even though I cannot say categorically who was missing, but most of them were there and the key personnel was already in the office with the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you involved in issuing of orders and the monitoring of what was going on, the assistance to the units that were out in the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Except for information, I was in no other way involved in the issuing of orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was your duty and function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we talk specifically of that morning, my duty was to bring in all staff members of the press service and radio. And many of them were non-professional. There were -- some of them were even not of age, and it was clear that a number of them would not be able to make it because shooting was going on all over the place. There were explosions coming from all sides, and it was very important to stem the panic that was spreading, because the telephones kept ringing all the time and people were calling in to ask what was going on and what they were supposed to do. This is why we decided, and the commander agreed to this, to rush and put together first information, and with the help of our staff to bring people who were involved in the press service and the radio and television to come and report to work. So I drafted the first information for the citizens, something that would also be a bit comforting. And members of the police force of our brigade were able to bring in several staff members of the local television and radio that were all grownups, so we were able to broadcast the first views around 9.00, even though -- and we were trying to calm people down even though it was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the next following days, what happened with you? Were you still involved in the disseminating of information or were you involved in other things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exclusively in information, and nobody asked of me to do anything else. Nor I could do anything else during that period because at that time it was literally full-fledged war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in the command post the whole time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Day and night. I had an office which was also a press service centre, and during the day there were two or three additional people there who were involved in the radio and television, but after they left I was -- I stayed behind to prepare everything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see when the arrest of Muslims started and where were they in relation to where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult to remember each and every detail in time and space, but I think it was on the second day that in the Croatian centre, which used to be called the Workers' University, that Muslims began to be brought in from the territory of the town of Vitez. Therefore, within this building there was a cinema hall and some other premises, so that some people decided, the people who made such a decision, that this was a suitable facility for detaining able-bodied Muslims from the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the conditions like in the cinema hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions certainly were not very good in terms of accommodation, because there was a large number of people in a relatively small amount of space. However, it -- from a different angle they could be said to be satisfactory, because there were no restrictions on the movement of those people. Their family members could come and visit them because this was in the centre of town, and they were, most of them, living a couple of hundred metres away. Food could be brought to them. If anyone needed medical attention a physician would come from the nearby medical centre or the person would be taken to see a doctor in the medical centre. By way of illustration, let me say that the toilet, the WC, which had two sinks that could be used for washing hands, were used by both the detainees and us, members of the command and personnel of the press service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were people mistreated? Were the detainees mistreated? Did you witness any physical mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can assert categorically that there was not a single case of physical mistreatment in this building, with the exception of the detention itself. But I can allege that there wasn't a single Muslim detained in the Workers' University who was mistreated or who experienced anything bad in addition to the fact of detainment itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Several days later an agreement was reached on an exchange of the Muslims detained in Vitez for Croats detained in Zenica. Do you know anything about that exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That exchange was to have been implemented. However, it was not fully but only partially, because already on the 16th Croats had a great deal of problems in Zenica, especially members of the Jure Francetic Brigade. First Commander Totic was taken into custody. Then on the 16th some members of this brigade arrived in Vitez, having escaped from there, the Jure Francetic Brigade, claiming that the Croats there, and especially HVO members, were having many problems. Many of them on the 16th, and later this tendency escalated, on the 17th and 18th, that is people were captured in their homes or in the streets and taken into captivity at the music school. This is a building housing the music school. The Muslims had an advantage in Zenica, an advantage figuratively. They had a large correctional facility where they put up the detained Croats. Excuse me. However, a negotiation started already on the 16th on a cessation of hostilities and on an exchange of detainees, because from one day to the next the number of detainees increased. One must say this applied to both sides, that is Muslim detainees on the Croatian side and particularly detained Croats who were far more numerous, in Zenica. As far as I know, the negotiations on our behalf were conducted by Boro Jozic, a good friend of mine who is also, unfortunately, deceased. The Croatians acted fully in accordance with the agreement reached. However, the detained Croats of Zenica did not come to Zenica as agreed, they remained in captivity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that the Croatian side acted fully in accordance with the agreement, does that mean the Muslims were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From this location that I was in, that is the Workers' University, most of them were either released to go back home in Vitez itself. Some of them wanted to go elsewhere, specifically to Zenica, some of them to Mahala, but this was mostly implemented in a correct fashion. And where our command was, the detainees were mostly the most prominent Muslims of Vitez municipality. In fact, most of them were my acquaintances. Some of them were friends of mine of many years standing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Muhamed Mujeznovic was detained there also, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Muhamed Mujeznovic, a prominent Muslim from Vitez, president of the War Presidency, and he was, in fact, one of those friends of mine that I worked with for many years. We worked together for 18 years in the Vitezit factory, he, as a specialist of internal medicine and a specialist of occupational medicine, and I as a social worker, were a team in the struggle to prevent disability in this large factory, the largest in Central Bosnia. As a result, our friendship developed to such a degree that we exchanged visits, private visits, in our homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him -- just a moment, please. I'm listening to the translation, so make a short pause to allow me to put the question to you. Did you see him in the premises of the Croatian centre and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did see Dr. Muhamed Mujeznovic together with the others. This was one morning. I think it was on the second morning, the 17th, and I was most embarrassed when I saw him together with the other Muslims, though I didn't like seeing them either, because as I said, most of them were very good acquaintances of mine and some very good friends. I did not communicate with Dr. Mujeznovic that very same moment, but immediately I climbed up the steps to see the commander, Mario Cerkez, and to ask him to allow me to take Dr. Mujeznovic home, to release him. At first, though Mario too knew Dr. Mujeznovic very well because Mario too used to work in the same enterprise as Dr. Mujeznovic and myself, he rejected my request because he was not the one who had ordered the arrest of Muhamed and the others in the Croatian centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who had given those orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure who, because this was in no way linked to the Vitez Brigade, except for the fact that they were accommodated in the same building as the command of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Muhamed Mujeznovic released and did he resume working after some time or do you know the exact date when he was released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I may be wrong, whether it was the 17th or the 18th, but it was one of those two days. In the afternoon of that day, the day I saw Dr. Mujeznovic and when I asked the commander Mario Cerkez that we should release him, radio Sarajevo and, in the evening, the television of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or Sarajevo television, in its news programme featuring the conflict in the Lasva Valley, reported, among other things, that in Vitez a prominent Muslim and a prominent physician , Dr. Mujeznovic, had been cruelly murdered in Vitez. This prompted me to try and affect his release with Mario once again, because Mario was not following the news broadcast by radio and television Sarajevo. On the other hand, that was my duty, to follow those news reports and to occasionally inform my commander, Mario Cerkez, of those reports. Late in the evening of the 17th or the 18th, I insisted once again with Mario that we release Muhamed, because I really felt extremely embarrassed whenever I passed and saw him and he would see me. Mario Cerkez asked me, "What are we going to do with Muhamed?" And I said, "What else could we do? What else could a doctor do in a war like this?" because there were many wounded and sick people. What else could he do except to perform his regular duties in the medical centre? Mario agreed, and about 22.30 or 23.00 hours I went downstairs to the room where Dr. Mujeznovic was, and I called him out from among a group of people. He came up to me, I told him to come with me. Of course, I made no other comments. I couldn't talk to him in front of the others. As we were climbing the stairs, I held him with my right hand, I held his upper arm in a friendly fashion, and I could feel that he was shivering, that he was afraid. At one point he asked me, "Zvonko, where are you taking me?" And I answered, "Surely you don't think I'm taking you for execution." Of course, I smiled, and this was an indication for him of my good intentions. I took him to the office of the Vitez Brigade commander, Mario Cerkez. Muhamed exchanged greetings with Mario. He sat down. Mario offered him a cup of coffee and some drink, and Muhamed accepted. We explained to him that we expected two things of him. The first was that the very next day, in the morning, he go to work at the medical centre and do his professional duties. He accepted with the greatest pleasure, as could be seen from the expression on his face. The second thing I asked of him was that, if he could, that he should deny on our local television, by appearing on television and by speaking, that he hadn't been killed. He was surprised to hear this, and he was ready immediately to appear on the local television because we could enter the satellite programme at any point in time because we were re-broadcasting this satellite programme and we could interrupt the satellite programme with our own feature and with our own images. Sometime around midnight, we did that, after making several announcements on the programme telling our citizens to expect an important information about midnight. We felt that having made this announcement, both Muslims and Croats would watch the programme because the news about the killing of Dr. Muhamed had an extremely negative impact in Vitez. Around midnight, Muhamed did briefly denounce the report of Sarajevo Television and took advantage of the opportunity to call on citizens, both Croats and Muslims, to be reasonable and to work for peace and said roughly that all that was happening in Vitez and the Lasva River Valley would benefit only the third party, and he meant the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any threats made to Dr. Mujezinovic in any sense since, according to his testimony, he was required to call up certain military commanders on the Muslim side to halt the attack on Vitez because of the existence of the explosives factory because the attack on Vitez on the 16th and 17th became very fierce.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether this was before he appeared on television or immediately after that, but Ivica -- Ivan Santic, the head of the municipality, and I think it was Pero Skopljak, the President of the Vitez HDZ, came to the command, and they greeted Mujezinovic very warmly, they shook hands, and they supported Mario Cerkez's and my decision for Muhamed to go to the health centre and work there because that was the logical thing to do. That was when the proposal or, rather, the request was made to Muhamed that he call up his friends, and especially a very good friend of his who was head of the medical detachment of the 3rd Corps of the BH army, he was a doctor -- I can't recall his name just now, but maybe I will later on -- he was also a specialist, a friend of his, to call him up and to tell him that the shelling should stop, that the persecution of Croats in Zenica end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The shelling of Vitez from all sides. Shells were falling on the town and the surroundings from all sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From which positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly from Grbavica, Bukve, Preocica, Sljivcica, and Vrhovine. These were villages mostly in the north of the municipality, but there were also shells coming from the area of Kruscica, Vranjska, and Rovna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the greatest problem in the event of the shelling of Vitez? What could have happened? Something very untoward for the whole area of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume you are referring to the factory. The factory was like an atom bomb in many respects. First there were the remains from the production of nitro-glycerine, and I think I don't need to dwell on what that means because a drop of it can provoke an explosion. There were large quantities of explosives, large quantities of poisonous acids, sulphuric and nitric acid and others, then there were large steam facilities, and all of this combined with nitro-glycerine and explosives could be like bombs that could destroy the whole of Vitez because the factory had a very large capacity of production.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When this request for stopping the shelling was made to Mujezinovic, was he threatened in any sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I can claim that emphatically because I would not have allowed, in my presence, any threats to be made to Dr. Muhamed because he was my friend. Regardless of the fact that we split on political grounds, we remained friends. I am glad to meet him even today, though many are not glad to see me communicate with him. Many people see him as an enemy. I do not because he was a longstanding friend of mine regardless of all the political differences between us. Later on, I tried to help his family, and I think succeeded up to a degree, because they emerged from the war safe and sound. He was simply asked to do this. The people who know Ivan Santic also know that he is not prone to threats or violence or coercion. Muhamed was merely asked to bring influence to bear on his friends to stop the shelling because a disaster could be provoked because of this factory; and secondly, because the shelling and killing were provoking reaction among the people exiled from Zenica whose children had been killed, to massacre or kill the detainees; and it was along those lines that we spoke to Muhamed, without any threats, because we knew that no threats would be of any avail because he was not in a position to do anything anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please take a look at this list of dead soldiers of the Viteska Brigade on the 20th of April and a list of the wounded of the Viteska Brigade. You wrote it, so I think you will probably be able to recognise it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D39/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cilic, will you tell us, please -- this is a document of the command of the Vitez Brigade. You are mentioned as the signatory, though you did not sign this document, but you are named here as assistant commander for information and political activities. It is a list of members of the Vitez Brigade killed in the conflict with the Muslims, and there are 23 names on the list. Tell us, are these all soldiers who were killed in the area of Vitez in the fighting during the first few days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. These are all soldiers, citizens of Vitez municipality who were killed in Vitez municipality. There is not one of them who did not live in Vitez or who did not come from Vitez. But there is a minor error here. All the killed listed here did not belong to the Vitez Brigade, but this is something I didn't know at the time. Some of these, I think a smaller number, I would not be able to identify all of them by name, came from other units, but the information that reached me and the names I received prompted me to place them in this list as members of the Vitez Brigade because at that point in time, what was important was the fact that they had been killed, so that no one insisted in particular on checking to make sure 100 per cent whether each one of the killed soldiers was a member of the Vitez Brigade or not. I know now that several were not members of the Vitez Brigade and yet they are on this list of 23 names. The same applies to the list of 63 wounded men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said these were members of other units but also from the territory of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, mostly from the territory of Vitez, though there may have been some from the territory of Busovaca or Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am saying units that were in Vitez at the time. I'm not saying where they had come from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this an official final list or was this just a report addressed to the information office of the operation zone of Central Bosnia, like a working document? Could we call it that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a draft report, and the task of all those working on similar assignments as myself in the Lasva River Valley in any one of the brigades or units had the same task, to draw up their own lists for their own units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you compiled this list on the basis of information that reached the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, information reached us. Later on, we established that this was in error, that they were not all members of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why does the name of the father not figure each time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't know at the time, and how could we, because there was no proper structure or organisation for us to be able to identify and check each and every name, and especially as some of these surnames in the Lasva River Valley are very widespread, and there are a large number of people with the same name, and only knowing some other personal data can they be identified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then there is also a list of wounded soldiers of the Vitez Brigade. There are 63 names on this list. So again, we have the same situation. Members of the Vitez Brigade wounded during those couple of days in the area of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but with the same reservation, that on this list too, there are names of men who were not members of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, who came from other units; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps this would be an appropriate time for a short break. I only have the final part of my examination-in-chief to do after this. I have a video to show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: How much time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Half an hour. All right. So we will take a break now, 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I would just like to request that the witness again be shown the document D39/2 because there is a further clarification that I think is necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to make this completely clear, and since we may go back later during the proceedings, could you tell us about the names on the list of the killed and wounded, who were and who were not members of the Viteska Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will only mention the names that I'm completely certain about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Just those who you know for sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Zlatko Ivankovic, Zeljo Livancic, Ivica Zepackic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Give us the numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please also mention the number when you read out the names of these persons mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 5, Zlatko Ivankovic. Number 8, Zeljo Livancic. Number 11, Ivica Zepackic. Number 15, Josip Slipac. Number 17, Zoran Bajo. Number 22, Mirko Popovic. For these I'm certain, and there are a few others that I'm not certain about and I don't want to make an error.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To which units did they belong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them were members of the military police and some others were the Special Purposes Unit members. They were from Nova Bila. Those were called Lightnings, and the others I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Special Purpose Units that you named Mujne, were they part of the Viteska Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, none of the Special Purpose Units were within the make-up of the Viteska Brigade, nor did the Viteska Brigade have any group of soldiers intended for this kind of special purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you also look at the list of the wounded and tell us who do you recognise from that list who was not a member of the Viteska Brigade but of other units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid that it would be much harder, especially because there is no name of the father beside the name, so I'm afraid that I could make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But for some of them you think that they were not members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If you look at -- ask me to look at the list in detail I will find a number of them who were not members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us about someone for sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you could just give me a little time to look. Number 17, Jako Opacak was not a member of the Viteska Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What brigade was he a member of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was a member of the military police, but you can take this with reserve because I'm not a hundred per cent sure. Number 55, Adis Cosic was also not a number of the Viteska Brigade. I think he was also a member of the military police. I think the same applies to number 52, Anto Krizanac. That would be about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Out of these 23 could you determine who were members of the military police and who were members of other units, and which units out of the 23 killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 5, Zlatko Ivankovic was a member of the military police. I think the same goes for Livancic Zeljo -- Zeljo Livancic. Also Ivica Zepackic. I think number 15, Josip Slipac was also a member of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Zoran Bajo and Mirko Popovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think Zoran Bojo was a member of the Special Purposes Unit, but I'm not sure whether he was a member of Munir or Tvrtkovci. Also, I'm not also a hundred per cent sure about number 22, Mirko Popovic whether he was a member of the military police or some other formation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are the rest soldiers of the Viteska and other units, with the information about the other units not being definite because you said this was primarily regarding the Viteska Brigade? Were there any other victims in those days among the civilians, and are there any civilians on this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there are no civilians on this list, because the lists of the killed and the wounded from the ranks of the civilians, this was done by the municipal civilian defence who also made lists and gave them to the Red Cross and the offices of the Viteska Brigade, and particularly to the office of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would also like to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D40/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the operative announcement from the Viteska Brigade, dated April 16, 1993, which was obviously written by the commanding officer of the brigade, the operative officer. Did you see this operative announcement of his?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it, and I used parts of it for information that we made -- that I provided to the local media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says in the statement that the citizens were in a panic and that they were constantly requiring information and asking advice. In order to -- that we had no contacts with the organs of civilian protection because they could the not make it to their places of work and were not answering their house telephones because they were in shelters. It also says that together with two officers there were also two police officers on duty at the start of the attack. Two of them went to the command of the regional police and then after that all traces of them are lost. They did not come back but they also did not reach the police. So this announcement indicates there was complete panic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If you recall when I spoke at the beginning of this session about preparing information for citizens, I said that the telephones were ringing off the hook because the citizens were asking for any kind of information about what was going on in Vitez and what could they do. The reason for this situation was the fact that the officials -- the workers, employees of the local radio station, could not arrive to work in time because this could not be expected due to a lot of firing, and detonations and shooting from light artillery, so that only late in the morning they started to arrive, the first employees from the press service began to arrive. You can see from this that the same situation was with the Civil Defence and other organisations and institutions in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It also says here that most of the officials of the command of the military units did not arrive to their post and there was disorganisation among their ranks. It also says that attacks were going on from all sides and there were no commands and no instructions. Was this your impression also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The situation was more or less like this. I said that a number of the command members, when I arrived, were already inside. Also, there were a number of officers on duty. Some of them arrived earlier, among them the commander. Also, he arrived before I did. But a number of the members of the command staff who lived a few kilometres away from the command post could not arrive immediately, so they came with a considerable delay to the command post of the Viteska Brigade. It is true that there was disorganisation in the ranks. I speak for myself first. I didn't know what to do at that moment. I felt the need that I had to do something, but I didn't know how or what would be the most effective thing that I could do. Simply, none of us were in that similar situation before, and it was very difficult, in general chaos, among the shooting and the explosions from all sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is another combat statement, communiqué. It was issued on the same day, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D41/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it very well. We -- parts of this report were used for our information that we passed along, and I think this report pictured very well the situation in the region, in the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you whether you can explain why this seal of 23rd of January, '93 was placed on this document. How is it possible that this seal is here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean this one in the upper right-hand corner? I think it's a little difficult for me to explain that. I didn't notice it immediately but it would be logical to conclude that the defence section received this report. I don't understand why this date, the earlier date, is on the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you can't explain why this stamp has this date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at the content. This combat report, signed by the officer on duty, in the English translation also we don't see the signature. Do you remember who was the duty officer on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. I think perhaps there were four of them. So it was very difficult to say which one was on duty. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is cited that the hand-launched 120-millimetre grenades were probably sent from the village of Preocica, and they fell very close to the post office and the command post of the Operative Zone. It then says, from the direction of Vjetrenice and Vrhovine, Muslim forces fired on Croatian houses in Poculica. The inhabitants of this village panicked, are frightened, and they've been calling to ask what to do as their homes have no cellars. The building of primary school Dubravica where Vitezovi are located is also being fired at. Muslim forces have opened heavy artillery fire on our settlements and units from Vranjska. So these would be the areas of attacks, and it is also cited that a mortar shell hit a prefabricated building on the grounds of the football stadium and some houses in Komarnjaca (phoen) were hit also. So these would be the areas of attack that you spoke about earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. If I can also say, the mortar shells which are cited here as having dropped around the post office and the command post of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone and in the immediate vicinity of the command of the Viteska Brigade, the mortar shells continued to fall in that region for the next eleven months. Hundreds of them were dropped. Because this location of about 150 metres, all the key institutions, the political ones of executive government and the military were located, I mean, the post office, the police, the municipal headquarters, the seat of the municipal authority, the command post of the Operative Zone, the Viteska Brigade, radio-television, so this was a logical place for constant attacks, particularly with grenades, mortar shells, and later with tanks as well. There are videotapes about this as well, information. A lot of people were injured in this area and a lot were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is one last document. If you could please look at it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before we move on to the next document, I wonder whether you might, by asking a question of the witness -- Mr. Cilic, if you compare document D40/2 and D41/2 and the numbers. On top of each document, you have "Strictly Confidential" and a number. Now, it struck me that D40/2, which was sent at 7.00 a.m., carries the number 02-125-9/93, and then the other document, D41/2, which was sent two hours later, at 9.00 a.m., carries the number -- or the reference 02-125/9. So can you explain why one carries the 9/93, the other one just 9? The following one has only this reference to 9. Should it be 9/94 or 10? I don't know. If you could clarify this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if I will be able to clarify this, although I agree with you that it should logically be so. But after the operative command officer makes the report, he gives it in handwriting to the secretary who typed it, and then after his signature, she would give it to the commander. What system of document registration this is, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Because in a way, in the indication of the incoming documents, there is more logic. You have the one sent at 7.00, which carries the number 293-4 or 7, and the following one, sent two hours later, carries the number 293/4/8. That means that it was a subsequent document, although, of course, there is an inconsistency in the date. Of course, I'm aware that the date is not consistent, but the number is consistent, this number of the receiving -- the incoming document. Anyway, thank you for your clarification. Thank you. Sorry, counsel, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would also like to ask you, relating to the Presiding Judge's question, if you can look at document D39/2. So if you would look at that? These are also different numbers, so if you can explain how these documents were marked according to the sub-numbers? Because here also there is a sub-number. They all have the same number, but they also have sub-numbers, just like the Presiding Judge said. Could you explain this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I will explain -- if I will manage to explain this completely, but I think that the sub-numbers relate to the services which wrote the reports. This seems to be the only logical answer because I am not familiar with the way of marking the documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I asked you about the date. The date is not appropriate, the date with the same stamp is on document D40/2, which you have. The stamp is the same, the handwriting is obviously the same. It was sent on to the Defence unit -- department on the same day. Is it possible that there is a mistake between documents 40 and 41, or maybe it's written illegibly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's difficult to conclude that a mistake like this could happen, but everything is possible, and I can't decipher this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, the stamp again has a sub-number 293-4-7. This is document D40. And D41 has 293-4-8, which follows. So there are some additional numbers. They were obviously sent on the same day, according to the numbers. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You can see that there's a sequence in this, and the way that the documents were received, they received the sub-numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. There is another operative report of the 17th of April, so if you could look at that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D42/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you managed to read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is something on the other side as well. I don't know if you noticed. In this part, the situation is described of 17th of April, '93, and item 2 is of interest to us where it is cited that the region of the Santici village, there was combat all day. The intensity of combat activities was especially pronounced after Muslim forces joined in from the direction of Sljivcica, Sivrino Selo, and Pirici with a constant artillery support from the direction of Poculica and Vrhovine. The goal of Muslim fighting was to take control of the Santici region, provide support from Zenica, and cut off the Kaonik-Travnik road stretch and join with the Muslim forces in the region of Rovna, Vranjska, and Kruscica as successfully as possible. Was this something that was known to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Any information like this was known to me, and from the beginning of the war until the end, each information of this kind, each combat report, passed through my hands, so this one did too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also item 2 states: From the direction of Zenica toward Kuber, it was observed that Mujahedeen and other extremist Muslim forces were on the move. Their task was to take control of the Kuber region and then with the support of artillery ordinance make a breakthrough on the stretch Gola Kosa. I can't -- this section is illegible. ... Kratine, join with Muslim forces and cut off the Kaonik-Travnik communication and join Muslim forces in the Rovna region. Was this information, as part of this report, was that also something that was known to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I especially remember this part of the report, and I have already stated this before. On the afternoon of the 15th, there was the first serious incident in the area of Kuber on the side supervised by members of the HVO from Busovaca. It is also easy to remember the events in Kuber because Kuber was the highest point held by the HVO, and strategically, it seems to me, that's what military experts said, it was very important because the Kuber point, you could see with your bare eyes Zenica and Busovaca, I mean the centre of the towns, so this was a very important dominant point for this region, and for this reason, attacks on this area were understandable, and on this day, on the 17th, the Muslim forces overran the most important and the most dominant part of Kuber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Could you please tell us when negotiations started on the cease-fire and calming the situation in Vitez at the highest military level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they started already on the 16th. Negotiations on the first day, in the afternoon, and then from day in, day out, they proceeded with immediate positive results which were of very short duration, and it was easy to conclude that there were no serious negotiations or no serious agreements reached. In spite of the fact that at some moments it seemed as if there would be a cease-fire and the horrors of war would stop, we would always be wrong, and then as far as I understand, already on the 16th in the afternoon, with the mediation of representatives of the British battalion which was stationed in Bila in the region of the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether any agreement on a cease-fire was reached on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there was a cease-fire agreement, and I think in an hour or two, there was a cease-fire, which looked very nice, but already in the evening hours everything resumed with the same force and tempo that it had in the morning hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Commander Blaskic issue orders to cease combat activity on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that in the evening, we already had the order by Tihomir Blaskic, which was a result of the agreement between Blaskic and Mr. Dzemal Merdan from the 3rd Corps, but you could take this name with a little bit of reserve because I'm not quite sure whether it was him but I think it was him. We received cease-fire orders which we took very positively, most of us, but this did not last long, unfortunately. The order was explicit, that weapons were not to be used against members of the BH army except in case our units were attacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. One additional document. This is the first attempt to calm down the situation, and this is an order for a cease-fire. I think those two documents are linked, so if we could look at both of them, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this report reach you about this meeting with Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I see it now, and I see that I made a mistake about who attended the meeting, but I was not wrong about the date when these negotiations were held, and I now recall some additional details about the whole process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says that; "HVO requirements: offensive operations, actions by Muslim forces in Vitez are to be stopped; abducted commander of the Jure Francetic brigade, Mr. Zivko Totic, is to be set free; abducted members of the HVO brigade headquarters from Novi Travnik are to be released." The most important information came from Colonel Stewart; "namely, that Commander Totic was alive and may be expected to be released perhaps this very day. This is being taken care of by UNPROFOR in Zenica." And the conclusions reached at the meeting were: "Cessation of fire, separation of forces, release of prisoners, care for the wounded, UNPROFOR patrols in towns and surrounding villages, and meetings to be held 17 April, '93, at 9.00 hours." Do you recognise Commander Blaskic's signature and stamp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Everything is in order here and I recognise it all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you recall the information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
