utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The relevance of your questions relating to Valenta?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It seems that most of the testimony of Mr. Cilic has dealt with explaining what process, political and military, existed, which led to the armed conflict in the month of April 1993 and what were the first episodes of this conflict in April 1993. However, the Prosecution does not share the point of view offered by Mr. Cilic, and it seems a number of questions must be asked in order for Mr. Cilic to give us his viewpoint on other issues which also may lead to an explanation for this conflict in April 1993, and therefore, if you will, a direct explanation of the context in which these accused acted within the context of the indictment, and so I believe this is quite central to the issue of this trial and not at all outside of the margins. This is why I have asked this question about Anto Valenta which I feel to be quite pertinent and relevant, if I may say so in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In light of what you have just stated, I believe indeed that your questions are relevant, and you may continue with your line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cilic, it was stated by Mr. Radovic that Mr. Valenta was a very high-level personality in Vitez and in Bosnia in general; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he occupied high positions in the political and executive power after the establishment of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like to mention another person whose name you mentioned during the examination-in-chief, that is Mr. Midhat Varupa. Who was he, Midhat Varupa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Midhat Varupa was a lawyer, a prominent lawyer, in the Vitez municipality, who worked in the same enterprise as I did. Though he was younger than me, we were very good friends, and I suggested, when I was given the opportunity to form the press service of the government in Vitez, I offered a post to Midhat Varupa because earlier on he had shown some gift for writing in the local media, and I was not mistaken in inviting him to join.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday, if I remember well, that Mr. Varupa left you. Without giving us any further details, can you tell us when and under which circumstances and for which reasons Mr. Varupa left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really will not be able to tell you the reasons for his leaving, unfortunately, but he came to our working meetings less and less frequently. These meetings were held in preparation for the local bulletins and the radio news programs. He would explain himself by other commitments because he was widely exploited, to put it that way, because he was a good lawyer and everyone wanted him to participate when any kind of decisions were being taken that were relevant for the Muslim people at the time. However, I personally can tell you that I remained a good friend of Midhat Varupa, and I was his guest for Bajram in 1993 because he was president of the Muslim cultural society, Preporod or Rebirth, and I was president of the Croatian cultural society, Napredak, in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have no memory of the reasons and the circumstances under which he left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it could be explained as follows: the worsening relations between Muslims and Croats in general and the formation of Croatian institutions of government in Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the only explanation that you have for this separation, this departure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I could add, but this is something I cannot assert with certainty, maybe he was given such instructions not to participate any longer in an information service, the radio and television, because we were using exclusively the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand. You're saying that he wasn't capable of speaking Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was capable, but I assume he didn't want to, because the Muslims, as the political situation worsened, I'm not saying that they were not right, but they felt this to be less and less their language, and this was a period of awakening of the Bosniak nation and, within that context, the Bosniak language, because according to the 1991 census, population census, 95 per cent of the population of Muslim faith declared their nationality to be Muslim and a very small percentage of them declared that they belonged to the Bosniak nation. Later on, the idea developed and was more generally accepted of the Bosniak nation and the Bosniak language and then there was no place, in my judgement, for the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cilic, is it true that Mr. Varupa refused to sign a document of allegiance to the HDZ, and due to this fact, he had to leave, under threat of weapons, his work post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have heard talk about certain requests for signing this allegiance, but I can claim resolutely that I never saw any such document, and I am quite confident that no one lost his job as a result.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have only answered half of my question. Did he leave his job under threat of arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to Mr. Varupa afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my sincere sorrow, Mr. Midhat Varupa was killed I think on the 16th of April, 1993, close to his apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Close to his apartment or in his apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was close to his apartment, but I'm not quite sure, so -- I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that this was the only Muslim killed in that part of town at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Several others were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, would you like us to have a break, or shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cilic. I said earlier that a large percentage of your testimony dealt with explaining the origins of the armed conflict from the month of April -- in the month of April 1993, under which conditions this was triggered and how it developed in the first days after the rest of April 1993. You stated, and I'm going to try to summarise what you've stated, giving substance, and you may correct me -- or you may tell me if I understood you correctly, you stated that under the circumstances of the war, during the Serb aggression in Bosnia, the impression was that they did not feel protected, they felt their security was not ensured and guaranteed, and given the attitude of the Muslims with regards to this Serb aggression in the -- at least in the first days, in the first part of 1992-1993, and that the attitude of the Sarajevo authorities at this time, in order to secure their security, the Croatian community at this time organised themselves and defended themselves, and this attitude, on the part of the Croatian community was poorly understood and poorly accepted by the Muslim forces in Bosnia, and that led to the armed conflict in the month of April 1993 which was initiated by the Bosnia-Herzegovina army. Of course, this is the summary of what you have stated to us, but did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle, yes, even though in order to make this statement even more relevant, some additional information may be added to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This is indeed a summary, and I was not perhaps able to be completely faithful to what you made in your statement, but I would like for us to look at a number of facts. A culmination of all of these facts, if you agree, could perhaps be an explanation for the war of April 1993, and perhaps may even characterise the logic of the war which was inevitable, and may explain in very broad terms the armed conflict of April 1993 between the Croatian community and the Bosnian army. I would also like to call your attention to a number of points, re-establishing in them in their chronological order. I would first like to, along with you, re-examine what the ideology was in 1992, the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, among the Bosnian Croats, what were the general ideas that they had, political ideas and national ideas that were held by the Croatian community, and I would like to -- not by referring to any dense (interpretation unclear) images, but rather to refer to publications that were made. One publication, which I found to be quite interesting in this regard, was made by Anto Valenta. You stated earlier, with regards to Anto Valenta, that he was an influential person. In 1991 he published a book on the political situation in Bosnia, and in particular, on the future politics of Bosnia. Do you know this work? Tile title is "The Partition of Bosnia and Its Conflicts." "The Partition of Bosnia and Its Political Future." Perhaps I would like to give a summary in a few sentences, if you will, to give you the thesis of this work which was developed in this book written in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just a moment, please. This witness at no time mentioned this book, not even whether he knows of it. The only thing he said was something in respect of Anto Valenta, which is that they knew each other and then he said that he was in a certain position. So I believe he should be asked whether he knows of this book and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Actually, it was a misunderstanding, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We may authorise the -- in cross-examination the -- to go beyond 90(H). Yes, to go beyond what was discussed or touched upon in the examination-in-chief. It's Rule 90(H); "Cross-examination shall be limited to the subject matter of the direct-examination and matters affecting the credibility of the witness. The Trial Chamber may, in the exercise of its discretion, permit inquiry into additional matters as if on direct-examination." I think in this case it is relevant. So you may proceed, Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I am not here to interpret Mrs. Glumac, but I believe she's also interested in knowing when Mr. Cilic knows of this book put out by Mr. Valenta, and Mr. Cilic just indicated to me said that he does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say, Mr. Cilic, that one of the theses of this book was that the ethnic mixing of those ethnic groups at that time would necessarily lead to civil war -- rather, necessarily lead to civil war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you want my personal view on this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cilic, I would simply like for you to confirm whether the sentence I just stated reflects well the thesis developed in this book by Mr. Valenta which you know and which you have read. That's all I wish to know for now, and after that I will go further. I simply wish to know now whether it is true that the thoughts of Mr. Valenta, as expressed in his book, is that the ethnic blending in Central Bosnia, in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole, would necessarily lead in a more or less long-term to civil war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Mr. Valenta's book quite well. It is called "The Partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Fight for it's Unity or Wholeness." Several theses were submitted there. One was moving the people from one area of Bosnia-Herzegovina to another, so resettlement in order to create ethnically homogenous areas, but some other ideas were also propounded in this book, and it was explained and elaborated in Anto Valenta's own words. In other words it reflected his own positions, and this was not the position of any institution or organisation of Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do the personal thoughts of Mr. Valenta, and I'm going to state them as the following six proposals: First, first of all, three nations divide up Bosnia. Second proposal, that in all municipalities in Bosnia these three nations blend together. The third proposal, that in all of these municipalities within Bosnia, one of these nations would hold the majority. The fourth proposal, that in -- that the situation change in 1991, the situation changes, says Mr. Valenta, due to the higher rate of propagation of the Muslim population in these municipalities, and, therefore, they could acquire the majority. The fifth proposal, the Croatians are in the majority in a number of municipalities, including those three groups of municipalities, including, of course, Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca and a number of others. Mr. Valenta also made up a map including the groups which would be useful in the course of a negotiation in Geneva at the end of 1992. The sixth proposal, it would be appropriate to hold and to promote ethnically pure and homogeneous regions through resettlement, something you mentioned a minute ago. Now, this resettlement of populations, which would be appropriate to encourage, would enable for these to become ethnically pure and to prevent civil war. Of course, there are other theses developed in this book, but what I've just defined, is it not, from your own perspective, the main thesis of this book, and, therefore, the opinion of Mr. Anto Valenta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how competent of an opinion I can express, but I can agree with you that these conclusions could be drawn from that book. In fact, the International Community, at one stage, was considering similar things. I think that that was expressed in the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will come back to that in a moment, but now I'd like to ask you two other questions. Did it not seem to you that in the beginning of the year 1993, the thoughts, as they were expressed by Anto Valenta, changed very little, and that they radicalised very little as well? I'm not talking about the substance but, rather, about the urgencies and the means to carry out the plan that he proposed. And I'm referring now to a document, the 26th of June, 1993, which was written. Are you familiar with this particular text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume you talk about the amended edition, the enlarged edition of this book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, this is a written document. Yes, indeed, it was amended as you said, but this is a document which translates to a certain type radicalisation -- or conveys radicalisation on the part of the author and is shared by more and more people, because the cohabitation of the two groups, in particular the Croatian community and the Muslim community, is less and less bearable. This indeed, the sentiments that were being conveyed in this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, Anto Valenta's book and ideas expressed in that book were never an official position of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and as a confirmation of that was the referendum about the unity of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And had the Croats not voted for that -- voted yes in that referendum, Bosnia-Herzegovina would not exist, because their votes helped Bosnia-Herzegovina stay together. This idea expressed in Anto Valenta's book was never that relevant, even at the level of the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. But in the month of June 1993, did Mr. Valenta not complain that the Muslims of Zenica, that is to say the Muslim authorities in Zenica refusing to carry out an exchange of the populations to move the Muslims from Busovaca to Vitez, and to move from apartments and houses which belong to Croats, and to move Croats from Zenica to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I believe Ms. Glumac has a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President. I would just like to say that Anto Valenta is on the witness list, and any questions about what Anto Valenta thought, because we are talking about Anto Valenta's opinions, in other words, what he thought, how he reacted to certain events, I believe can be asked of Mr. Valenta himself by Mr. Terrier, because this witness said that he did not share his views because he did not share -- and he did not read Anto Valenta's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry, I did not know -- I didn't have that previous information about the witness with regards to this trial, so without trying to interpret Mr. Cilic, I believe he stated and I believe he can confirm this for us, that he was personally not in agreement with this. He said simply that this was an official thesis -- rather, this was an unofficial thesis, and is this true, Mr. Cilic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm certain for my own one hundred per cent, and I know that that was never an official position or an option that was considered officially. Maybe amongst some individuals but not officially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I should now like to go on to another area, to try and make progress in explaining the conflict of 1993, and that is the circumstances under which the defence council of the Croats was formed and how it developed. Would you agree with me in saying that the Croatian defence council was formed in November 1991, and at the time the war had not ended in Croatia and that there was no war in Bosnia at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that your information was not accurate. I don't want to make a mistake, but I think that the HVO was not established in November of 1991, but rather in April of 1992, but the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna was established in November of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was talking of the HVO. It can be -- I was calling -- I was referring to the Croatian defence council which can be identified with the HVO, and it was formed in November '91 by constituent congress held on the coast. You said that you know that the founding movement of the Croatian nation in Bosnia started in November '91, and that is for me what is most essential in any event. Would you agree with me in saying that the Croatian defence council or the organisation of the Croats in Bosnia was constituted in November '91 and then it developed in '92 and '93 into a state, a legal state separate from all the other existing authorities in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have the accurate information here. As I said, on 4 April, 1992, the Croatian Defence Council was established. However, the question you just asked, I believe that in some aspects, the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, and later on Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, did have certain attributes of a State, but if you will allow me, if I am permitted to not agree with your view that the Croatian side did not recognise the official authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina; I would rather say that there was no official authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina because the official authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina could only mean equitable relations of Croats and Muslims and, if you will, Serbs. But if you take into account that the Serbs voted against Bosnia-Herzegovina, the government could not view the aggression of Serbs against parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina which were populated by Croats as a State should view any aggression against any part of its territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. But nevertheless, let us look things from a -- you are speaking from a legal point of view, but from a political point of view, in an attempt to explain the conflict of April '93 and the submission I'm making to you and on which I should like to hear your opinion is the following: From the beginning of November 1991, did the Croatian community of Bosnia not form itself as a legal State with all the attributes of a State, of a modern State: that it had legislative powers, executive powers, administrative powers, and a very broad range of control in the economy, in the sector of education, transport, communications, and, of course, in the area of defence? Is it true to say that that community constituted itself as a modern State?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that in some aspects, it looked like a State, in certain structures of government. However, you're looking at it from a legal standpoint, and we were involved in it in a vital way. It had to do with the survival of Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the survival of Bosnia and Herzegovina itself, and perhaps in that sense one should try to see how things were at that time when the Serbian forces, which had one of the largest standing armies in Europe, when they were trampling over Bosnia, and the authority in Sarajevo still viewed it that this could still be considered as they put "our" army with some minor corrections in its chain of command, and I'm sure that Bosnia would not have survived had certain Croatian institutions not been established which ensured the defence and prevented the Serbs from overrunning the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cilic, we have a copy of Narodni List, or the official gazette of the HVO, and we have examined a large number of legislative texts published in that official gazette, and we have discovered a certain number of things, such as repeated reference to the Croatian dinar, the currency of the Republic of Croatia, which was preferred to the Bosnian currency. Then one also notes that the curriculum in elementary and secondary schools was modified to use school textbooks used in Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me in saying that the political logic which is behind the development of a state of this kind is necessarily in the long term secession, independence, or even attachment to another republic, but in any event, secession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all. I don't think that you could interpret it in that way, and I will attempt very briefly to clarify this. Would that mean that we should have continued to use the Serbian language, to use the Serbian dinar, study Serbian history, or, as you call it, Bosnian dinar, which was printed day and night and had absolutely no value and it was just a means to draw the last hard currency reserves from the Croatian people and even from the Muslim people? At that time, the German mark was the most important, and why did they not keep it? But Croatian dinar was bothering everybody because -- some policemen even were overturning stalls in marketplaces where Croatian dinar were used. Muslims also used Croatian dinar because all logistic supply went through Croatia and this dinar could be used by them. They could not go to Serbia but they could go over there to Croatia to re-supply themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, could you go on to some other questions that will be less general and more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, I will try to do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cilic, would you agree with me in saying that a State, in a situation when its security is not guaranteed, needs a flag, an army, and a territory, and that that army was constituted by decree, a decree that was published and implemented in the normal manner, in the principle of a levy in arms, that all the citizens have a duty to defend the independence and territorial integrity of the Croatian community; did that principle exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that the Croats embraced this principle of the first, to protect Bosnia from the Serbian aggression, which was clear to the whole world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I come to the question of territory. You referred a moment ago to the Vance-Owen Plan proposed in January 1993; that plan envisaged the formation of provinces: three Serb provinces, three Croatian provinces, and three Muslim provinces, including the town of Sarajevo; do you agree with that? The Croatian community of Bosnia accepted immediately the Vance-Owen Plan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We agreed to this plan, that is, the representatives of the Croatian people accepted this plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the other hand, the authorities in Sarajevo were more hesitant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This hesitation on the part of the authorities in Sarajevo prompted the Croatian authorities to feel irritated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if you could call it that way, to be bothered or irritated. It may not be my place to comment on these positions, as you put it, the official Croatian position on Bosnia and Herzegovina, but it is obvious that the Muslim side hesitated because, as it turned out later, it had different plans and different appetites, and it was not satisfied with what they were offered by the representatives of the International Community. They felt -- and this is my personal view, of course -- they felt that they could gain from Croats what they had lost from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that at the beginning of April 1993, an ultimatum was addressed by the Croatian authorities in Bosnia to the authorities in Sarajevo to immediately implement the Vance-Owen Plan and also to withdraw the Muslim troops from the provinces attributed to the Croats under the Geneva plan, and specifically, from the region of Vitez and Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of such an ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shall like to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this document is a dispatch by Reuters which refers to this ultimatum of the Croatian authorities. Unfortunately, I only have it in the original, that is in English, and I couldn't have it translated today into the Croatian language, but perhaps, if you accept, we could read just two or three very brief passages to refresh the witness's memory.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 333.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cilic, please accept my apologies. I was not able to have this document translated into Croatian. It is a dispatch of Reuters dated 4th April, 1993, and I'm going to read to you a very short passage so that you could tell us whether this refreshes your memory.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have a copy. Could they have a copy, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is indicated that the Bosnian Croats demanded the withdrawal of Muslim troops from provinces designated as Croatian under the peace plan prepared by the United Nations which revived tensions between those who were officially allies, who were officially allies at the beginning of this year. The HVO, on the 15th of April, 1993, therefore, addressed an ultimatum or a deadline to Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic, to sign a joint communiqué ratifying the withdrawal of his troops -- this is understood -- and creating and certifying that no conflict would exist regarding territory between Muslims and Croats. Finally, it is stated, quoting a Croatian official: "If Izetbegovic does not sign this agreement by the 15th of April, the HVO will unilaterally enforce its jurisdiction in cantons three, eight and 10." Therefore, it appears that the existence of this ultimatum -- obviously, there will be other sources and other testimony to confirm this -- that at the beginning of April 1993, the Croatian authorities decided if, by the 15th of April, the Bosnians did not sign the actual implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan negotiated in Geneva, they would take the initiative on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for reading these passages, but my memory has not been refreshed, and I do not believe that I would have failed to remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. We question the authenticity of this news report. If the Prosecutor believes that there is a document called an ultimatum, then we can accept it, so that we know that an ultimatum was given. Respectable news agencies such as Reuters or CNN also make mistakes, and from this Reuters information, it is not clear whether their correspondent ever saw this ultimatum. So if there is an ultimatum which was officially issued, it must exist in respect of archives, and there is no problem in getting this document from them since they've been so cooperative with this Tribunal anyway. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It is very clear from the fourth paragraph of this document, of this Reuters report, that it was not an ultimatum but it was an "ultimatum-like statement" carried by Croatian State media, so therefore it is a journalistic classification of the statement as an ultimatum. As to the value of this report, I think the Prosecutor is right in trying to use it just to ask the witness whether or not he remembers the facts reported here. So, therefore, we don't need to check whether this particular report is authentic or not. It is based on a statement which was issued by the Croatian State media. The statement will probably, I hope, be produced by the Prosecution, the actual statement, which is defined here as an "ultimatum-like statement." So, therefore, I think the Prosecutor is right in asking this question of the witness. You may proceed, Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It seemed to be rather credible and appropriate to submit to the witness a dispatch of Reuters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to ask you several questions now regarding the arming of the HVO army. This question was mentioned during your examination-in-chief, I think, on the first day, and specifically a document which I think carries the number D17, in which there is information saying that weapons captured in a JNA barracks were shared -- I think it's document 17, I'm not quite sure -- that the weapons seized in establishment of the JNA were shared between the Territorial Defence and the HVO, and this occurred at the beginning of May 1992. At the time, the Territorial Defence in May 1992, could it have been considered as an auxiliary force or the principal force of the Muslims in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at that time, the Territorial Defence was a military force of the Muslim people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In truth, though, there were members of other ethnic groups in it at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was an inventory made of the weapons seized from JNA institutions and which were distributed in this way? Was there an inventory, or did you see a report saying what kind of types were involved, what kind of weapons were involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, I had no access to military units, and I do not know whether any inventories were compiled, but I know that no side had any serious objections to the division or distribution of this seized equipment and weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your point of view and on the basis of your experience, was that the way in which the HVO was armed? Was that how anti-aircraft guns were procured, such as we have discussed in the course of this trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I did not understand you well, so if you would please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Gladly, Mr. Cilic. My question was as follows: Was it in this way, seizing the weapons of the JNA, that the HVO was armed? Was that how anti-aircraft guns were obtained, the guns that were widely used in the course of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those weapons were also seized in some of the depots of the former JNA, but let me underscore again that it was distributed 50-50 between the Muslims -- that is, the TO and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember a truck transporting weapons coming from Croatia to deliver them to the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please specify your question further, because as you are putting it, I cannot really give a satisfactory answer to your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To me, the question appears to be quite specific. Let me repeat. Do you know that any trucks full of arms came from Croatia to Bosnia to deliver them to the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know of any specific truck, but it is certain that weapons did arrive from Croatia for Bosnian Croats, but the Muslims received them too. Both Croats and Muslims were supplied from Croatia as well as from the former JNA depots in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I go now to the events of the 15th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, excuse me. I assume that you still have quite a number of questions to address to this witness. We cannot finish the cross-examination this evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So you are going to begin a fresh series of questions regarding the events of the 15th of April. Could we postpone this for Friday so as to allow the Defence attorneys to deal with the question of your list of witnesses? Then we have ten minutes to deal with that issue, and you can continue your cross-examination on Friday. We hope that we will be able to finish by 1.30 p.m. Friday with this witness and maybe even proceed to the next one. So I should like to ask Mr. Pavkovic to present to us in very succinct terms the objections of the Defence regarding this document of the Prosecution dated 12th January.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I announced these comments at the initiative of my colleagues, I thought that only the Defence counsel who had any objections would submit them themselves rather than my summarising it for them, and with your permission, it is going to be pretty brief. Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence of Vlatko Kupreskic received the Prosecution list in which the Prosecution objects to ten witnesses. We believe that we cannot meet the request, and we specify it as follows. In the case of four witnesses, we never took witness statements of these witnesses, and these include the President of the Supreme Court with whom we only spoke of whether he was prepared to come and testify here to explain the practice on the Bosnian law and testify to a single specific judgement regarding war crimes. With respect to this witness, we have no further statements. Also, another summary was for a witness which is a Muslim woman. At that time, the Trial Chamber ordered that no contact be established between the witness and the Prosecution. This witness should only testify about the authenticity of a videotape and whether she moved along the path indicated in the videotape, and we consider it unnecessary to take a separate witness statement from her, so that even to date, we do not know what her testimony will be. We just wanted to show her the videotape here in the open court and ask her to comment on it, and this is why we cannot provide any additional materials there. A further witness will be called here only to authenticate a signature on a document. We never talked to him. We only asked him if he would be prepared to come and testify. So that was in the summary of our text. As to the other witnesses, we provided their statements. They contain everything that we want to talk to them -- to examine them on, they may last no more than ten minutes each. Whether a particular accused was seen by them at a particular time and in a particular place. In that sense, we believe that we have nothing further to offer to the Prosecution, and we, therefore, ask the Trial Chamber to relieve us of an additional obligation to provide further material. We say that we have provided everything that was necessary and everything that will be part of our examination of these witnesses and, therefore, ask for this relief. I would also like to use this opportunity to announce that the accused, our client in this case, will take the stand and testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Would you, Counsel Par, indicate on this list the witnesses you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: In that case I would ask for a closed session, because some of these witness may be protected witnesses, so I would rather not read out their names. I'm referring to the list of the 12th of January. There are no numbers. Perhaps we could say these are witnesses listed at the bottom of the page, from the last name on this page and ten witnesses up the page. From the bottom upwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: On this column, on the left column.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: From the bottom upwards. In the first column, yes. In the left-hand column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So the last ten witnesses at the bottom of the first column on the left-hand column?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Objections from other Defence counsel? No other Defence counsel? So the other Defence counsel, I understand, are prepared, therefore, to provide within two weeks more detailed statements. Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I received a request from the Prosecution to enlarge the statements, and I have done so. However, according to the new list, I see that three more witnesses have been added to this list. They are Vlado Alilovic, Jadranka Tolic and Dragan Stojak. However, these statements have to do with the general part of the indictment. That is, they will testify about the relationship between the Muslims and Croats before the conflict, after the conflict; before the elections, after the elections; and they will testify about the first and the second conflict. So I think it would be superfluous for me to explain at any great length what they're going to testify about, because we are talking about these things every day. So I think it is not necessary for me to expand their -- the summaries of their statements, but if the Court insists, I will do that. As for the others, I have provided more details, but these are brief summaries, and their statements have to do only with confirming that Drago Josipovic was in a particular place. The witnesses need not testify what Josipovic did in various other places when he was at a different place, and that is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: One further point. We have come to the conclusion, on the basis of our experience, that he went beyond the scope of the statements made by the witnesses when they were called here in court, so that they went beyond those statements that were given in advance to the Defence and to the Court in their examination-in-chief of the witnesses they called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you kindly mention again the three names you mentioned before? One is Dragan Stojak, and the another two?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Vlado Alilovic in the first place, and Jadranka Tolic, under number 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mrs. Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I also have an objection. We have listed and given relatively satisfactory reports about all witnesses, about 40 or 50 statements, and there were not many objections, but there are a number of witnesses of our witnesses (sic), character witnesses for whom we have received questions. They're not talking about the circumstances of the acts, but they are listed as character witnesses. They are Franjo Rajkovic, Ljljana Sapic, and Emin Parinda, and Ivan Taraba. So these are witnesses, if we call character witnesses, particularly all of them, they will be talking about the character traits of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. So I it think there is no need to give any detailed statements or summaries, because obviously they will be speaking about their own contacts with them. So I think that the request of the Prosecution regarding these witnesses is not acceptable, and we have separated them into a separate group. As for other character witnesses, we have given their written statements, their written depositions, because we don't know whether they will be appearing in court. But for these others, as they are character witnesses, we feel that there is no need to provide their statements. Also, regarding the statements of Ivica Kupreskic, with respect to the statement of Ivica Kupreskic, we have provided a summary of that statement, including the data that he gave to us. So it simply explains where he was on the previous day, on the 16th and on the 17th, and I consider that to be sufficient, so I would ask you to rule in that sense, if possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, have you any comments to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: A very brief commentary, Mr. President. I would simply like the Defence counsel to understand that our only concern is to be able to prepare properly, in the interests of justice, for the cross-examination, as for the witnesses whose names appear on the list for whom we do not have sufficient elements. If this causes enormous difficulties for Defence counsel, I would be ready to examine with them a compromise solution. For example, we can meet with those witnesses in their presence. I have no intention of exerting any pressure or influence on those witnesses. It is simply a matter of knowing what's going to happen, what is going to be the gist of their testimony, and I would like that to be quite clear. It was in this spirit that we made this request, but not to exert any pressure on anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Now, let us quickly go through the various witnesses mentioned by Defence counsel. First of all, let me start from the bottom, say the ones mentioned by Counsel Slokovic-Glumac. I understand, if I understood you correctly, most of them or all of them are character witnesses, the ones you mentioned. For them we would like, again, to insist with you, with all Defence counsel, that you should use, as much as possible, Rule 94 ter, affidavit evidence. Why don't you turn those statements into affidavits so that we don't need to call those witnesses here? Mostly because you are not sure whether some of them are prepared to come over here to give evidence in court, so it will be the best solution, if, of course, the Prosecution does not object to those affidavits, they could be admitted into evidence. Now as to the other ones mentioned by Counsel Par and Counsel Susak, I think the Prosecutor is entitled to having as many elements as possible for the cross-examination, because under Rule 73 ter you, the Defence counsel, must provide a summary of the facts on which each witness will testify, and of course, there is a sort of inherent sanction for cases of non-compliance with this Rule, namely that the Defence counsel will not be entitled to ask questions going beyond facts mentioned in the summary they have already produced or they will produce. So, therefore, it is probably in your interest, if you want to ask questions in examination-in-chief, to at least, in a summary fashion, to indicate the facts on which they are going to give evidence. However, if you are not in a position to provide detailed statements, at least you should tell -- notify the Prosecution of the facts on which you intend to examine the various witnesses in chief so that the Prosecutor is in a position to do so. And probably also the solution, Mr. Terrier just indicated of, namely, contact. The possibility of a Prosecutor interviewing a witness, in your presence, just to ask about what facts he's going to testify on. This might also be a solution. But you may prefer to provide more detailed statements. There's also the question of the Judge. I think we should try to know as much as possible about the subject of his testimony. We would like to have some sort of summary statement from the Judge you intend to call. Yes, Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, I think that we have fulfilled our obligations. I would suggest that for each of these cases that we say we have provided all the elements that we will examine the witness on in the cases when we have supplied the statements. In the cases where we have supplied summaries, we have provided summaries as to the facts the witness will testify to. We have not discussed those facts with the witness, and we don't know any further details. Let me repeat again an example. We spoke to the President of the Supreme Court. Surely we're not going to question him as to the way in which he's going to explain the judicial practice in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He will submit a previous judgement and discuss it. So I would propose, for the cases or the names that are disputed in our case, that the Prosecutor tells us exactly what additional information he needs, but it was our position that we have fully complied with the obligations under the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Right. Now, as for the President of the Supreme Court, I understand that he will simply comment on the judgement, the judgement you have already provided. I read a judgement. So therefore, he will confine himself to commenting on that judgement. All right. I think the Prosecutor will be happy with this solution. But I would welcome, along the lines you just suggested, some contacts between the Defence counsel and the Prosecutor, maybe tomorrow, so as to verify matters and sort out points which are still under discussion, and this way we would come to some sort of solution. Final point, what about the list of witnesses you have decided no longer to call? Remember, the Prosecutor asked to be provided with such a list? Do you think you could provide such a list, say, by Friday? Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will obviously have to consult with my colleagues before answering that question. I still have not finalised my list. I am in touch with the witnesses, and if I would personally have to tell you today, I would not be able to do that, but I shall try to respect the deadline you set in your ruling, and I think the other colleagues will do the same. Whether we'll be able to do that by Friday I'm not sure, but in any event, by the deadline you have set we will do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. I think we -- are there any other matters to be discussed this afternoon? There are none, so we adjourn until Friday at 9.00, and we'll be sitting from 9.00 until 1.30, and there is no sitting on Monday, as you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: at 5.40 p.m. to be reconvened on Friday, the 15th day of January, 1999 at 9.00 a.m.
